name: Teke Kingdom (Anziku)
summary: A kingdom of the Teke on the plateaus north of Malebo Pool, trading partner and rival of Kongo; King Makoko signed a treaty with Brazza in 1880 that started French Congo.

location.value: The Teke (Batéké) plateaus north of Malebo Pool on the Congo River, in today’s Republic of the Congo; the royal town Mbe lay on the plateau.

terrain.value: High, sandy grass plateaus cut by river valleys such as the Lefini, with strips of gallery forest along the streams.

climate.value: Tropical savanna climate: hot all year, with a long rainy season and a dry season in the middle of the year.

resources.value: Copper from the lower Niari region traded through Teke lands, raffia cloth, ivory, cassava and fish from the rivers and Malebo Pool.

disasters.value: Not well recorded; droughts, poor harvests and epidemics probably struck from time to time, as across the region.

population.value: Not known; the plateaus were thinly settled, and the kingdom probably had tens of thousands of people at most.

urbanisation.value: Mostly villages; a royal or market town.

migration.value: Not well recorded; traders and their dependants settled around Malebo Pool, and captives were moved along the river trade.

economicBase.value: Farming of cassava and other crops, hunting and fishing, and above all middleman trade at Malebo Pool between upriver and coastal traders.

tradeRoutes.value: Teke traders at Malebo Pool linked Bobangi canoe traders from the upper Congo with caravan routes to Kongo and the Atlantic coast.

wealth.value: Moderate; chiefs at Malebo Pool grew rich from ivory, slave and cloth trade, while the plateau villages stayed poor.

moneyAndTax.value: Tribute, cloth, cowries and trade goods.

inequality.value: Rulers and nobles above farmers; captives and slaves at the bottom.

governmentType.value: A sacred monarchy headed by the Makoko (king), with much real power held by territorial lords and chiefs.

keyRulers.value: Makoko Iloo I, who signed a treaty with Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza in 1880; earlier kings are known mostly from oral tradition.

succession.value: The kingship passed among royal lineages; a new Makoko was chosen and installed by senior lords rather than by strict father-to-son rule.

institutions.value: Territorial lords and village chiefs governed their own areas; the Makoko kept ritual authority linked to the national spirit Nkwe Mbali.

stability.value: Long-lasting but loose; by the 1800s the king held mostly ritual power while lords and Pool chiefs competed for trade.

eliteConflict.value: Lords and chiefs at Malebo Pool sometimes competed with each other and with the Makoko over trade and tribute.

armyAndTech.value: No standing army; lords raised followers armed with bows, spears and knives, and some guns came through trade in the 1800s.

majorWars.value: Portuguese sources describe wars between Kongo and the Anziku (Teke) in the 1500s; details are uncertain.

territoryChange.value: The kingdom’s lands north of Malebo Pool came under French rule after the 1880 treaty and became part of French Congo.

alliancesRivals.value: Kongo was the main rival and trading partner; the Teke also dealt with Bobangi traders and, from 1880, with France.

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded; Teke smiths worked iron and copper, and weavers made fine raffia cloth.

scienceEducation.value: Oral learning; Qur’anic schools where Islam spread.

openness.value: Open to trade: Teke markets at Malebo Pool took in European cloth, guns and beads from the coast in exchange for ivory and slaves.

communicationTransport.value: Footpaths across the plateaus, canoes on the Congo River and Malebo Pool, and porters carrying goods to the coast.

religion.value: Traditional religion centred on ancestors, nature spirits and the royal spirit Nkwe Mbali; protective figures held medicine bundles.

languageWriting.value: Teke (Kiteke), a Bantu language with several dialects; no writing was used before European contact.

artsArchitecture.value: Wooden figures (biteki) holding medicine packs, carved masks, raffia cloth and copper ornaments; houses of wood and thatch.

socialStructure.value: The Makoko, territorial lords, village chiefs, free villagers and traders, with captives and slaves at the bottom.

sharedIdentity.value: A shared Teke language and loyalty to lineage, local lord and the sacred kingship of the Makoko.

dailyLife.value: Village farming; cassava, millet or sorghum.

neighbours.value: Kongo to the south-west, Bobangi river traders to the north-east, and other Teke and Bantu peoples on the plateaus.

ideasReligions.value: Sacred kingship: the Makoko was a ritual figure linked to the national spirit Nkwe Mbali rather than an all-powerful ruler.

colonisation.value: In 1880 Makoko Iloo I signed a treaty with Brazza that placed his lands under French protection and began French Congo.

riseSignals.value: The kingdom already existed by the 1500s, when Portuguese and Kongo sources first mention the Anziku north of Malebo Pool.

peakPeriod.value: Probably the 1500s–1600s, when the Anziku were a strong rival of Kongo; trade at Malebo Pool stayed rich into the 1800s.

declineSignals.value: Power slipped to lords and trading chiefs in the 1800s, and French colonisation after 1880 ended independent rule.

outcome.value: The kingdom became part of French Congo after the 1880 treaty; the Makoko title survives today as a traditional office.

overallCertainty.value: Known from oral traditions, travellers and colonial records; many dates are approximate.
